slides.title: How a quantum dot emits
slides.subtitle: From a few-level solid to a measurable quantum optical source
bullets: Section 2 · 30 minutes
slides.notes: This section builds emission from a confined semiconductor level up to the number a photon-correlation detector reports, and it insists on keeping three claims separate: a quantum device (3D confinement and Coulomb blockade, carrier quantum mechanics), a quantum treatment of the dot (exciton-phonon coupling, exciton-biexciton-trion structure), and a quantum treatment of the light (field quantization, g^(2)(tau), regression theorem) [Project's own treatment slides, slide 3]. The repository's own model sits at Level 2 of that hierarchy: a semiclassical rate-equation cascade with photon statistics attached through cascade identities, not a Lindblad master equation with quantized field modes [Fox, Quantum Optics (2006), ch. 8]. We follow the chain in order -- dipole coupling, Fermi's golden rule, the exciton-biexciton-trion ladder, the cap-2 rate equations fsim_core/cw_g2.py solves, Hanbury Brown-Twiss statistics, background dilution, finite loading, detector response, phonon sidebands, thermal linewidth broadening, and thermal carrier escape -- ending with the room-temperature landscape and what remains unmeasured. Every number carries either a citation to a published measurement, a repository module that computed it, or an explicit assumption tag; the goal is that nobody mistakes a design-sensitivity sweep for a completed device certification.

slides.title: What does ‘quantum’ mean here?

columns.heading: Quantum device
bullets: 3D confinement gives discrete carrier states.
Coulomb blockade controls charge occupancy.

columns.heading: Quantum treatment of light
bullets: Quantised field, Fock states, and operators.
Normally ordered g² tests the output.

slides.notes: The word 'quantum' does triple duty in this literature, and conflating the meanings is a common error in claims about single-photon sources [Project's own treatment slides, slide 3]. A 'quantum device' means only that carrier motion is quantum mechanical: three-dimensional confinement gives discrete electron and hole levels, and Coulomb blockade fixes how many charges can occupy the dot at once. Neither property says anything about the emitted field. A 'quantum treatment of the light' is the separate, stronger claim that the electromagnetic field itself is quantized -- Fock states, ladder operators [a, a-dagger] = 1 -- so photon correlation functions such as the normally ordered g^(2)(tau) become well-defined observables rather than heuristics [Loudon, The Quantum Theory of Light]. A device can be a genuine quantum device (confined, blockaded) while its light is described entirely classically; conversely, establishing g^(2)(0) < 1 requires the field-quantized description regardless of how classical or semiclassical the emitter model underneath it is. This section keeps the two axes visually and verbally distinct throughout, since the repository itself only ever implements the first axis together with a cascade shortcut for the second.
sources: Loudon, The Quantum Theory of Light

slides.title: Quantum treatment of the dot versus the light
slides.notes: The table separates four analysis layers often blurred into one 'quantum dot' claim. The device layer is carrier confinement and Coulomb blockade -- levels and charge occupancy, no photon physics yet. The dot layer follows internal exciton/biexciton/trion states through either a rate equation or a master equation, giving populations and, at the master-equation level, coherences. The light layer quantizes the field itself: Fock modes, input-output theory [Gardiner and Collett, Phys. Rev. A 31, 3761 (1985)], and the quantum regression theorem, which actually produces g^(2)(tau) and Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility from a Lindbladian. The repository occupies the dot row's rate-equation branch: a semiclassical cascade (Level 2 in the owner's four-level hierarchy of rate equations, semiclassical, fully quantum, and output-state treatments) that reports purity and brightness through cascade identities rather than deriving them from field-quantized operators. That placement is not a defect to hide; it is why every g^(2) number in this deck should be read as a rate-equation regression result, correct on its own terms, but not a substitute for the Level-3/4 calculation the owner's brief names as the unclosed joint with electrical driving and 300 K phonon dephasing.

slides.title: What a single-photon source must meet

rows: p-i-n mesa drive; pump statistics enter photon statistics
InP dot in a GaAsP well; exciton near 1.88 eV (visible)
staged target 0.1 or 0.5: open program decision
collection efficiency is an EM-simulation item, outside this model
ambition; staged deliverable anchored at 77-120 K

slides.notes: The program specifies five independent conditions, and each demands something different of the model [Project's own treatment slides, slide 2]. (1) Electrical injection: a p-i-n mesa drive, so pump statistics -- not just pump rate -- must propagate into photon statistics. (2) An epitaxial III-V dot: InP dots embedded in a GaAsP well, a visible-wavelength platform with the exciton transition near 1.88 eV. (3) Purity g^(2)(0) < 0.5, with the staged target itself still an open program decision between 0.1 and 0.5. (4) In-plane SiN waveguide coupling: an integrated-photonics collection geometry whose efficiency is an electromagnetic-simulation problem, explicitly outside this semiclassical model. (5) Room temperature as the ambition, with the anchored, currently defensible deliverable staged at 77-120 K. None of these gates is optional and none substitutes for another: a device can be bright and still impure, or pure and still too dim, or pure and bright at the wrong wavelength for the waveguide. Reischle's electrically pumped visible-range device up to 80 K is the closest published analogue to conditions 1, 2, and 5 together, though not yet at 300 K [Reischle et al., Optics Express 16, 12771 (2008)].

slides.title: Light–matter coupling
bullets: H = −d·E
Interband dcv contains the Bloch matrix element.
Kane energy EP packages band-edge coupling.
HH/LH selection rules choose polarisation.

equations.latex: H_{int}=-\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf E,\quad d_{cv}=\langle u_c|e\mathbf r|u_v\rangle
equations.caption: d is dipole, E field, and uc, uv periodic Bloch functions.

slides.notes: The interaction Hamiltonian H_int = -d.E treats the confined interband transition in the electric-dipole approximation: d is the transition dipole operator and E the (here classical, later quantized) field. Its matrix element d_cv = <u_c|e r|u_v> factors into an envelope-function overlap set by confinement and a periodic Bloch-function part inherited from the bulk band structure. In III-V zinc-blende semiconductors that Bloch part is packaged by the Kane energy E_P, which sets the interband momentum matrix element magnitude common to conduction-to-heavy-hole and conduction-to-light-hole transitions [Chuang, Physics of Photonic Devices]. Confinement and strain lift the heavy-hole/light-hole degeneracy and mix the valence states, so which combination of u_c and u_v actually couples -- and with what polarization -- follows selection rules set by that mixing rather than by the bulk band edge alone [Yu and Cardona, Fundamentals of Semiconductors]. This dipole matrix element is the single quantity that, once squared and summed over vacuum modes in the next slide's golden-rule sum, sets the radiative rate Gamma_rad that everything downstream -- lifetime, brightness, the pulsed g^(2) cascade timing -- is built on.
sources: Yu and Cardona, Fundamentals of Semiconductors

slides.title: From golden rule to spontaneous emission
bullets: A dot lifetime is commonly in the 1 ns class.
Oscillator strength packages dipole strength.

equations.caption: n, ω, d, ε0, ħ, c are index, frequency, dipole, vacuum permittivity, reduced Planck constant, and light speed.
f is oscillator strength; m0 and e are free-electron mass and charge.

slides.notes: Fermi's golden rule sums the dipole-photon coupling over the continuum of vacuum electromagnetic modes and, after integrating the mode density, gives the familiar cubic-frequency spontaneous-emission rate Gamma_rad = n omega^3 |d|^2 / (3 pi epsilon_0 hbar c^3), with n the host refractive index [Fox, Quantum Optics (2006), ch. 8]. For the isotropic dipole magnitude |d| used in that rate, oscillator strength is f = 2 m_0 omega |d|^2 / (3 hbar e^2): it repackages the same dipole matrix element into a dimensionless number, not an independent measurement. The commonly encountered single-component convention omits the factor 3 because it assigns |d| to one Cartesian dipole component rather than to the isotropic magnitude. Self-assembled III-V dots typically show radiative lifetimes in the 1 ns class once envelope confinement and host index are folded in [Michler (ed.), Quantum Dots for Quantum Information Technologies (2017)]. The repository does not derive Gamma_rad from a microscopic dipole calculation; it takes radiative rates (gamma_X, gamma_XX) as model inputs, either class-proxy values or, where available, anchored fits to a specific dot's measured decay. This golden-rule derivation justifies treating gamma as a rate constant in the cascade equations that follow.

slides.title: Two-level atom versus quantum dot

columns.heading: Jaynes–Cummings
bullets: H contains one emitter and one cavity mode.
g exchanges excitations coherently.

columns.heading: Regimes
bullets: Weak coupling: Purcell enhancement.
Strong coupling: dressed states.
FP=(3/4π²)(λ/n)³Q/V.

slides.notes: The Jaynes-Cummings model -- one two-level emitter coupled to one quantized cavity mode with coherent exchange rate g -- is the simplest fully quantum-optical Hamiltonian and the natural point of comparison for a quantum dot [Michler (ed.), Quantum Dots for Quantum Information Technologies (2017)]. Two regimes follow from the ratio of g to the emitter and cavity loss rates. In weak coupling, spontaneous emission stays irreversible but its rate is modified: the Purcell factor F_P = (3/(4 pi^2)) (lambda/n)^3 Q/V quantifies how a high-Q, small-mode-volume cavity accelerates or, off resonance, suppresses radiative decay, which is the lever the repository's cavity block uses. In strong coupling, g exceeds the loss rates and the system instead forms dressed light-matter eigenstates with a vacuum Rabi splitting -- coherent, reversible exchange rather than a modified rate [Purcell, Physical Review 69, 681 (1946)]. A quantum dot is not, however, an ideal two-level atom even before coupling to a cavity: exciton, biexciton, charge, spin, and phonon degrees of freedom all sit on top of the single dipole transition the Jaynes-Cummings picture idealizes, and it is exactly those extra levels -- the subject of the next several slides -- that create the multiphoton and dephasing effects a bare two-level treatment misses.

slides.title: Exciton, biexciton, and trion ladder
bullets: 0 → X → 0 emits one X photon.
XX → X → 0 is a cascade.
ΔXX controls XX leakage through an X filter.

equations.caption: E_XX^ph denotes the XX photon energy, E_X is the X photon energy, E(XX) is the two-exciton complex energy, and Ebind,XX is the binding energy. Delta_XX = E_X - E_XX^ph = Ebind,XX is the X-XX spectral splitting used throughout.

slides.notes: The exciton (X, one electron-hole pair) and biexciton (XX, two pairs bound by Coulomb and exchange interactions) sit on a ladder: 0 -> X -> 0 emits a single X photon, while XX -> X -> 0 is a two-photon cascade. The biexciton binding energy shifts the XX transition below twice the exciton energy: E_XX^ph = E_X - E_bind,XX is the photon actually emitted on the XX -> X step, and E(XX) = 2E_X - E_bind,XX is the two-exciton complex's total energy [Bimberg, Grundmann and Ledentsov, Quantum Dot Heterostructures (1999)]. The quantity used throughout this deck as Delta_XX is exactly this spectral splitting, Delta_XX = E_X - E_XX^ph = E_bind,XX -- the energy separation between the X and XX emission lines, typically a few meV in InP-class dots. That separation is the only thing standing between a clean single-photon X line and biexciton leakage: an X-centered spectral filter narrower than Delta_XX rejects the XX photon, but as the homogeneous linewidth Gamma grows with temperature the two lines increasingly overlap and XX leaks through, which is precisely the epsilon = t_XX/t_X leakage fraction quantified two slides ahead [Michler (ed.), Quantum Dots for Quantum Information Technologies (2017)].

slides.title: Fine structure and entangled photon pairs
bullets: Exchange splits the bright-exciton doublet.
Fine-structure splitting rotates polarisation phase.
Near-degenerate paths can yield entangled pairs.
Pair fidelity and single-photon purity differ.
Here XX is mainly leakage.
slides.notes: Electron-hole exchange interaction splits the two bright neutral-exciton spin states into a doublet separated by the fine-structure splitting (FSS), typically tens of micro-eV in strained self-assembled dots. FSS acts as a birefringence for the biexciton-exciton cascade: it rotates the relative phase between the two orthogonally polarized decay paths (XX -> X_H -> 0 and XX -> X_V -> 0) as a function of the delay between the two emitted photons. When FSS is small compared to the radiative linewidth, the which-path information carried by polarization is washed out and the two cascade photons can be entangled in polarization [Akopian et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 96, 130501 (2006)]. This is a genuinely different objective from the single-photon purity this deck otherwise tracks: entangled-pair fidelity asks how well the two photons' joint state matches a Bell state, while g^(2)(0) asks whether more than one photon pair is emitted per trigger [Michler (ed.), Quantum Dots for Quantum Information Technologies (2017)]. In the repository's cascade model, XX is treated purely as a leakage channel degrading single-photon purity through the X filter; the fine-structure/entanglement physics on this slide is not implemented and is not needed for the program's g^(2)(0) < 0.5 target.

slides.title: Cascade rate equations
bullets: Pump r loads X and XX.
γ terms radiate; k terms escape.
generator and steady_state implement this ladder.

equations.caption: NXX is biexciton population; r pump; γXX radiative rate; kXX escape.
NX and N0 are exciton and empty populations; gammaX radiative rate; kX escape. Both radiative and non-radiative XX exits return population to X.

slides.notes: fsim_core/cw_g2.py models the exciton-biexciton cascade as a three-state, incoherent Markov chain on the ordered basis |0>, |X>, |XX> -- no optical coherences, appropriate when dephasing dominates Rabi coupling under incoherent electrical or above-band pumping. Pump rate r drives 0 -> X and pump_ratio times r drives X -> XX; each level empties radiatively (gamma_X, gamma_XX, emitting a photon) and non-radiatively (k_X, k_XX, thermal escape). generator() assembles the 3x3 rate matrix and steady_state() returns normalized occupations (P_0, P_X, P_XX). Detailed balance gives P_X = a P_0 and P_XX = a b P_0, with a = r/(gamma_X+k_X) and b = pump_ratio*r/(gamma_XX+k_XX). Both gamma_XX and k_XX route XX into X, so the X return flux is set by pump_ratio*r*P_X. Dropping k_XX instead raises P_XX and hence the XX leakage-photon rate I_XX; it does not increase the X return flux. The displayed equations therefore retain pump_ratio explicitly and conserve population [fsim_core/cw_g2.py].

slides.title: Photon statistics: what HBT measures
bullets: g²(τ) is normally ordered.
Classical fields obey g²(0) ≥ 1.
A single emitter recovers after a jump.
HBT records coincidence delay.
slides.notes: The Hanbury Brown-Twiss (HBT) experiment splits the collected light on a beamsplitter and cross-correlates the two detector click streams as a function of delay tau, estimating the normally ordered second-order correlation g^(2)(tau) = <a-dagger(t) a-dagger(t+tau) a(t+tau) a(t)> / <a-dagger a>^2. For any classical field -- coherent, thermal, or any statistical mixture of coherent states -- the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality forces g^(2)(0) >= 1; values below one have no classical-field explanation and certify a genuinely quantum state of light [Fox, Quantum Optics (2006)]. A single quantum emitter shows perfect antibunching, g^(2)(0) = 0, because after it emits at t=0 it has been projected into the ground state and cannot emit a second photon until it re-excites and radiatively decays again -- the dip's width and shape trace that re-excitation and decay dynamics [Loudon, The Quantum Theory of Light]. The figure plots this single-emitter antibunching dip against the Poisson (g^(2)=1) reference. In a real device, background light and finite detector timing resolution both lift the observed dip toward one, which is exactly what the next two slides quantify.
sources: Loudon, The Quantum Theory of Light

slides.title: Background turns a perfect dip upward
bullets: ρ=s/(s+b) is the signal fraction.
The background is independent and Poissonian.
integrator.g2_from applies the law; device.py and cw_g2 use it downstream.

equations.caption: s and b are signal and background means; ρ is signal fraction.

slides.notes: Real detection always mixes the dot's intrinsic signal with an independent background: stray pump light, other emitters within the collection aperture, or dark counts. If the total detected stream is signal (mean rate s) plus statistically independent Poissonian background (mean rate b), expanding the second factorial moment of the sum gives an exact mixture law for the measured correlation: g^(2)_meas(0) = 1 - rho^2 [1 - g^(2)_s(0)], where rho = s/(s+b) is the signal fraction [Reischle et al., Optics Express 16, 12771 (2008), Eq. (1)]. Even a perfectly antibunched source, g^(2)_s(0) = 0, is measured as g^(2)_meas(0) = 1 - rho^2 once background is present -- at rho = 0.9 a perfect single-photon source already reads 0.19, not 0. This is why every purity number in this deck must be reported alongside its rho, since a headline g^(2) can be made to look better simply by narrowing the collection window and discarding signal along with background. fsim_core/integrator.py's g2_from implements this law exactly, and both cw_g2.py (CW) and device.py (pulsed) apply it downstream of their respective intrinsic g^(2) calculations.

slides.title: Cap-2 Poisson loading
bullets: P0=e−μ and P1=μe−μ.
P2=1−P0−P1 after cap-2 relaxation.
loading.f1b_g2 carries finite-μ penalty.

equations.caption: μ is mean loading; ε=tXX/tX is leakage.

slides.notes: Pulsed excitation loads the dot with a Poisson-distributed number of excitons per pulse, mean mu; the repository caps the ladder at two excitons (0, 1, or 2, i.e. up to a biexciton), so P_0 = e^-mu, P_1 = mu e^-mu, and the remaining probability P_2 = 1 - P_0 - P_1 collapses onto the cap-2 state after fast intra-dot relaxation. Detecting a photon in the central (tau=0) peak of a pulsed g^(2) histogram requires two consecutive pulses to each contribute at least one photon; because the biexciton state leaks an XX photon through the X filter at fraction epsilon = t_XX/t_X, loading.f1b_g2 derives the closed-form pulsed peak-area ratio f_1b g^(2)(mu, epsilon) = 2 P_2 epsilon / [P_1 + P_2(1+epsilon)]^2 directly from these three occupation probabilities and epsilon [fsim_core/loading.py]. In the weak-pumping limit mu -> 0, P_2/P_1 -> mu/2 and the formula recovers the simpler F1 identity g^(2)(0) = epsilon; at finite mu it adds a genuine multiphoton penalty from double-pair loading on top of the spectral leakage penalty, the same physical effect Hanschke identified as making multiphoton probability grow with pulse area [Hanschke et al., npj Quantum Information 4, 43 (2018)].
sources: Hanschke et al., npj Quantum Information 4, 43 (2018)

slides.title: CW g² and quantum regression
bullets: The propagator follows a detected jump.
Low pump: g²dot(0)=εpSXX/SX.
cw_report returns intrinsic, background, and IRF curves.
CW and pulsed g² are different observables.

figure.caption: Fresh gainp-card rate-equation g2_meas(tau), plotted from -8 to +8 ns with 4 ps sampling.

slides.notes: Continuous electrical or optical pumping produces a steady-state photon stream rather than discrete pulses, and its g^(2)(tau) is obtained by a different route: the quantum regression theorem, which for the classical three-state Markov chain of the previous slides reduces to 'propagate the post-jump state forward under the same generator M'. After detecting an X photon the dot is reset to |0>; after detecting an XX photon it is reset to |X>; cw_g2.py's cw_report() builds both post-jump propagators, weights them by their steady-state photon rates and the filter transmissions t_X, t_XX, and returns the intrinsic curve g2_dot, the background-mixed curve g2_meas, and the IRF-convolved curve g2_raw together [Gardiner and Collett, Phys. Rev. A 31, 3761 (1985)]. In the low-pump limit this reduces to g^(2)_dot(0) -> epsilon * pump_ratio * (S_XX/S_X), the CW analogue of the pulsed F1 identity. The figure loads the fresh gainp design card (cards/edge-inp-gainp-design.yaml) at its own resolved 80 K and 300 K operating points -- pump rate, retention, escape, filter window, and background all recomputed from the card, giving g2_meas(0) about 0.23 at 80 K and 0.72 at 300 K -- and this is a rate-equation regression on a classical generator, not a field-quantized calculation; CW and pulsed g^(2) remain genuinely different observables of the same device.

slides.title: Detector response is part of the measurement
bullets: Measured g² is IRF-convolved.
erfcx gives a stable closed form.
A 5 ps dip is diluted by a 100 ps FWHM IRF.
Deconvolution is model-dependent.

equations.caption: A is dip depth, τd recovery time, σ Gaussian IRF width.

figure.caption: IRF broadening via convolve_irf, +/-300 ps window showing full recovery.

slides.notes: A photon-counting detector's finite timing resolution, its instrument response function (IRF), convolves the intrinsic correlation before it reaches the histogram. cw_g2.py provides both Gaussian and two-sided-exponential IRF kernels; convolve_irf() performs the numerical convolution on a uniform tau grid for the general case, while dip_convolved() gives a closed form for a single-exponential dip g^(2)(tau) = 1 - A exp(-|tau|/tau_d) convolved with a Gaussian IRF of standard deviation sigma: g^(2)_raw(0) = 1 - A exp(sigma^2/(2 tau_d^2)) erfc(sigma/(sqrt2 tau_d)), rewritten with the scaled complementary error function erfcx to stay numerically stable when sigma >> tau_d [fsim_core/cw_g2.py]. The figure widens the plotted delay window to +/- 300 ps specifically so the convolve_irf traces are shown recovering fully back toward g^(2)=1 at large |tau| rather than being truncated mid-recovery; at that scale a 5 ps intrinsic recovery time next to a 100 ps FWHM IRF is visibly all but erased, while a 20 ps IRF only partially dilutes it. Reischle's electrical HBT measurement used a roughly 500 ps exponential IRF and deconvolved it to recover 0.15/0.25 background-included dip depths from raw dips of 0.41/0.43 [Reischle et al., Optics Express 16, 12771 (2008)]; deconvolution is model-dependent and only as good as the assumed dip shape.

slides.title: Phonons I: sidebands and the independent-boson model
bullets: Acoustic phonons couple to charge density.
IBM resums diagonal coupling.
A ZPL sits on a broad sideband.
Temperature transfers weight to the sideband.

equations.caption: C is dipole coherence; Z is ZPL fraction; S is Huang–Rhys factor.

slides.notes: Acoustic phonons couple to the exciton through the deformation potential, which is diagonal in the exciton number (it shifts the exciton energy rather than flipping it), so the exciton-phonon Hamiltonian is exactly solvable: the independent boson model (IBM) resums the coupling to all orders and gives the dipole coherence C(t) = exp[phi(t) - phi(0)] in closed form, where phi(t) is a phonon correlation integral over the bath spectral density J(omega) [Krummheuer, Axt and Kuhn, Phys. Rev. B 65, 195313 (2002)]. Fourier transforming C(t) gives an emission spectrum with two pieces: a delta-function zero-phonon line (ZPL) of weight Z = exp(-S), where S is the Huang-Rhys factor, sitting on a broad phonon sideband carrying the remaining weight 1-Z. As temperature rises, more of the total spectral weight moves from the ZPL into the sideband -- the physical origin of the temperature-dependent linewidth broadening on the next slide. fsim_core/qd_gf.py implements this acoustic deformation-potential IBM lineshape, including ZPL weight and sideband transmission through a filter, but it does not yet include piezoelectric coupling (relevant for the (211)B InAs dots Chatzarakis studied), microscopic LO-phonon scattering, or the polaron-frame renormalization a coherently driven dot would need.

slides.title: Phonons II: linewidth grows with temperature
bullets: Γ(T)=Γ0+aT+b/[exp(ELO/kBT)−1].
Matsuda anchors Gamma(300 K)=12 meV; InP E_LO=43 meV.
Chatzarakis anchors warm-dot behavior.
The coded 300 K envelope is 6–20 meV.

equations.caption: Γ0 residual width, a acoustic slope, b LO coupling, ELO LO energy.

slides.notes: The phenomenological model Gamma(T) = Gamma_0 + aT + b/[exp(E_LO/k_B T) - 1] separates a residual width Gamma_0, a linear acoustic-phonon term aT, and activated scattering requiring a thermally populated LO phonon. With E_LO = 43 meV for InP, the activated term is negligible at low temperature but rises rapidly toward 300 K. Matsuda's In0.5Ga0.5As/GaAs single-dot measurement anchors Gamma(300 K) around 12 meV [Matsuda et al., Phys. Rev. B 63, 121304(R) (2001)], while Chatzarakis's InAs data constrains warm-dot behavior to 260 K [Chatzarakis et al., Phys. Rev. Applied 20, 034011 (2023)]. fsim_core/linewidth.py's gamma_envelope() deliberately encodes a class range rather than a single curve: its coded 300 K envelope spans 6-20 meV, reflecting dot-to-dot and material-class variation, not a measurement of the specific InP/GaAsP target dot. Measurement 1, a temperature-dependent linewidth on that target, has not yet been run.

slides.title: Band-gap and line shift with temperature
bullets: Varshni shift moves X and XX.
InP and GaAs do not walk identically.
A filter must track the selected line.
Drift changes brightness and ε.

equations.caption: E0 is zero-temperature gap; α and β are Varshni parameters.

slides.notes: The Varshni relation E_g(T) = E_0 - alpha T^2/(T+beta) captures the empirical, largely phonon-driven redshift of a semiconductor band gap with temperature; E_0 is the T=0 gap and alpha, beta are material-specific fit parameters tabulated for essentially every III-V binary and common alloy [Vurgaftman, Meyer and Ram-Mohan, J. Appl. Phys. 89, 5815 (2001)]. Because InP (the dot) and the surrounding GaAsP/GaInP matrix do not share identical Varshni coefficients, the exciton and biexciton transition energies drift at a different rate than the barrier and matrix band edges as the device heats from a cryostat baseline toward 300 K -- confinement depth itself is temperature dependent, not just the absolute transition energy [Yu and Cardona, Fundamentals of Semiconductors]. This matters operationally because any spectral filter or cavity resonance fixed at a room-temperature design wavelength will walk off the actual X/XX lines as the device self-heats under drive, and because t_X and t_XX (the filter transmissions that set epsilon = t_XX/t_X) both depend on where the lines sit relative to the fixed filter window -- a filter that is not re-tracked with temperature silently changes brightness and purity together, not independently.

slides.title: Spectral overlap sets biexciton leakage
bullets: Lorentzian lines pass through a window set to w=Gamma.
ε=tXX/tX is cascade contamination.
Larger ΔXX helps; larger Γ hurts.
spectral.epsilon feeds pulsed g².

figure.caption: epsilon versus Gamma for DeltaXX=4, 6, 8 meV; the sweep sets filter window w=Gamma.

slides.notes: spectral.epsilon() computes the leakage fraction epsilon = t_XX/t_X: the transmission of two Lorentzian lines, centered Delta_XX apart with linewidths Gamma_X and Gamma_XX, through the same acceptance window. In the swept figure the window width is tied to the linewidth itself, w = Gamma, rather than held fixed, which is why epsilon rises with Gamma along each Delta_XX curve -- a wider intrinsic line both broadens into the window from outside and needs a wider window to pass its own weight, so both lines increasingly overlap. Larger Delta_XX pushes the two lines further apart and helps suppress leakage at fixed linewidth; larger Gamma hurts, since the two Lorentzian tails increasingly overlap regardless of their separation -- the same competition between confinement-set Delta_XX and phonon-set Gamma that reappears in the 300 K landscape slide. At the worked point Delta_XX=6 meV, Gamma_X=Gamma_XX=12 meV, window 12 meV, the repository returns epsilon = 0.7048 [fsim_core/spectral.py: epsilon], a leakage fraction far above the 0.1-0.5 purity target and a concrete illustration of why 300 K electrical operation is hard for this dot class [Chatzarakis et al., Phys. Rev. Applied 20, 034011 (2023)].

slides.title: Thermal escape and retention
bullets: S(T)=1/[1+a e−Ea/kT+b e−Eb/kT].
Ea follows confinement and escape paths.
The presets are class proxies.
Thermal loss can cost 1000× brightness.

equations.caption: S retention; Ea,Eb activations; a,b prefactors.

slides.notes: Carriers confined in the dot can escape thermally before recombination. The retention fraction S(T) = 1/[1 + a exp(-E_a/k_B T) + b exp(-E_b/k_B T)] is the two-channel Arrhenius intensity-retention form reported by Chatzarakis et al. [Phys. Rev. Applied 20, 034011 (2023)]. Bommer et al. measured single-dot activation energies in InP/(Al,Ga)InP, providing an activation-energy anchor but not this two-channel retention form [J. Appl. Phys. 110, 063108 (2011)]. dot_levels.retention_params() derives E_a, E_b, a, and b from computed confinement levels rather than fitting them independently, tying escape to the same offsets and geometry used elsewhere. For the coded InP/GaAsP class preset it returns E_a = 83.79 meV under the module's pair-half convention: an assumption-class proxy, not a measurement of the target dot. Because S(T) multiplies brightness and falls steeply as k_B T approaches E_a, escape can cost orders of magnitude between cryogenic and room temperature, independently of linewidth-driven purity loss.
sources: Bommer et al., J. Appl. Phys. 110, 063108 (2011)

slides.title: Indistinguishability: the other quantum metric
bullets: HOM measures wavepacket overlap.
Phonons and charge noise raise γ*.
Low g² does not guarantee HOM visibility.
300 K indistinguishability remains open.
slides.notes: Purity (g^(2)(0) < 0.5) and indistinguishability are independent quantum metrics, and a source can satisfy one while failing the other. Indistinguishability requires two emitted photon wavepackets to overlap coherently, which depends on the emitter's optical coherence time T2, not on its population statistics: 1/T2 = 1/(2 T1) + gamma*, where T1 is the population (radiative) lifetime and gamma* is the pure-dephasing rate from phonon scattering, charge noise, and spectral diffusion. Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference measures this overlap directly -- two photons entering a beamsplitter from indistinguishable sources bunch into the same output port -- and its visibility falls whenever pure dephasing broadens the line beyond its transform-limited, radiatively broadened width [Iles-Smith, McCutcheon, Mork and Nazir, Nature Photonics 11, 521 (2017)]. Low g^(2)(0) says only that the source rarely emits two photons per trigger; it says nothing about whether those single photons are spectrally and temporally identical to each other. The repository does not compute the photon density matrix, T2, or HOM visibility anywhere -- an explicit, acknowledged Level-3 gap relative to the owner's four-level hierarchy -- and at 300 K, where phonon dephasing is strongest, indistinguishability is expected to be the harder of the two quantum metrics to close [Project's own treatment slides, slide 4].

slides.notes: This is not a continuous landscape. out/rt_edge/sweep.csv samples only a 2x2 grid: Gamma(300 K) = 6 or 20 meV and Delta_XX = 4 or 8 meV. Each cell contains 192 rows varying card, T_hs, IRF, NA, R_back, and L; the plot honestly summarizes their pulsed g^(2) distributions. Its cell minima are 0.437, 0.321, 0.763, and 0.653 respectively for (6,4), (6,8), (20,4), and (20,8) meV. The sensitivity remains design guidance, not a device measurement. Laferriere's optically pumped InAsP/InP nanowire dot reaches g^(2)(0)=0.57 at 300 K [Laferriere et al., Nano Lett. 23, 962 (2023)], while Deshpande's electrical 300 K result is g^(2)(0)=0.29 on nitride InGaN/GaN [Deshpande et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 105, 141109 (2014)]. No row combines electrical drive, 300 K, g^(2)(0) < 0.5 and an arsenide or phosphide epitaxial dot.

slides.notes: This table restates the owner's experimental-status slide: five results are the closest anchors to the program's conditions, but none simultaneously supplies the complete target platform [Project's own treatment slides, slide 7]. Deshpande supplies a 300 K electrical single-photon result on InGaN/GaN, not an arsenide or phosphide dot. Laferriere's optical InAsP/InP nanowire result rises from g^(2)(0)=0.11 at 77 K to 0.57 at 300 K. Chatzarakis supplies optical warm-dot X/XX context to 260 K. Zhao is an electrically driven 300 K QD-laser ensemble, not a single-photon source. The card reports 3.1 dB pump-current amplitude squeezing [cards/zhao.yaml], whereas the paper digest records 0.9 +/- 0.1 dB directly measured squeezing (6.7%) [paper_digests.md]; these are reported as different quantities, but the repository does not yet reconcile their discrepancy. Kitamura reports a resonant-tunneling-injection architecture without an extractable photon-statistics number. slides.title: How our model integrates this

columns.heading: Input physics
bullets: materials.py: gaps and offsets.
dot_levels.py: levels and retention.
linewidth.py and qd_gf.py: thermal response.

columns.heading: Measured output
bullets: device.py: injection and brightness.
spectral.py/loading.py: ε, μ, pulsed g².
cw_g2.py: CW correlation and IRF.
sde.py: Zhao pump-noise SDE, kept as an acknowledged failure (F_p proxy).

slides.notes: The repository's chain runs materials and confinement parameters (materials.py, dot_levels.py) into thermal optical response (linewidth.py's phenomenological Gamma(T), qd_gf.py's independent-boson lineshape), then spectral transmission, finite-pump loading, background dilution, and rate-equation propagation into device.py's reported brightness, purity, and injection observables. It is a Level-2 semiclassical stack with closed forms checked in verify/verify_<module>.py. One failure is kept visible: Zhao's stochastic pump-noise SDE reproduces the ordering of the two published g^(2)(0) points, normal and quiet, both at I = 4 I_th [cards/zhao.yaml], but does not reach the published squeezing magnitude under literature-bounded parameters. The separate number 12 refers to tuning experiments in scripts/run_zhao_fit.py, not measured operating points. device.py therefore bypasses the physical SDE and uses an empirical Fano-factor parameter F_p priced from Zhao's measured values [fsim_core/sde.py; fsim_core/device.py]. This exposes the unclosed field-level joint: a relay-hop rate model cannot carry electrical pump regulation into field statistics. Quantized modes, a photon density matrix, and Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility are absent; the next slide addresses that gap.

slides.title: What is left
bullets: Measure Γ(T) and ΔXX to 300 K on one electrical dot.
Demonstrate confinement and edge collection together.
Calibrate background, IRF, filter, and pulsing.
Add HOM visibility and electrical-pulsing data.
Treat the sweep as design guidance, not evidence.
slides.notes: Five items remain open, matching the slide bullets. First and most gating is Measurement 1: an actual Gamma(T) and Delta_XX distribution to 300 K on the electrical InP/GaAsP target dot. Second is demonstrating confinement and edge collection together. Third is calibrating background, IRF, filter, and pulsing. Fourth is adding HOM visibility and electrical-pulsing data. Fifth is retaining the sweep as design guidance rather than evidence. For the electrical arm, Kantner-style transport-to-Lindblad coupling would replace device.py's one-way injection parameters with a dynamical, bidirectional link [Kantner, Mittnenzweig and Koprucki, Phys. Rev. B 96, 205301 (2017)]. The staged 120 K, g^(2)<=0.1 target with a large-lens dot, quiet high-impedance rail, and 10-12 pair DBR, and the 77 K slit-filter/no-cavity target, are from the owner's slide 9 [digest-qd-quantum-treatment.md]. The actual current repository verdict is FAIL with evidence=incomplete and conditional=true [out/rt_edge/verdict.md], so those staged targets are not a simulator verdict.

slides.title: Section summary
slides.subtitle: Emission is a chain: ladder → coupling → statistics → temperature limits
bullets: Discrete states do not alone certify quantum light.
Purity combines loading, leakage, background, and IRF.
Temperature couples linewidth, escape, and filter alignment.
Next: electrical injection and edge-emitting device physics.
slides.notes: We built the chain in order: the dipole Hamiltonian and Fermi's golden rule set the radiative rate; the exciton-biexciton-trion ladder and its cap-2 rate equations set the population dynamics; Hanbury Brown-Twiss statistics, background dilution, finite-pump loading, and detector-response convolution together set what a real measurement reports versus what the intrinsic dot produces; phonon sidebands, thermal linewidth broadening, Varshni line shift, and thermal carrier escape set how all of the above degrade as temperature rises toward the 300 K target. The distinction carried through every slide is the owner's own: a quantum device (confinement, blockade), a quantum treatment of the dot (exciton-phonon coupling, cascade structure), and a quantum treatment of the light (field quantization, g^(2), HOM) are three different claims, and satisfying one does not imply the others [Project's own treatment slides, slide 3]. The repository's validated stack sits at Level 2 -- a semiclassical cascade with photon statistics attached through exact mixture and cascade identities -- and every number in it traces to a repository module, a cited measurement, or an explicit assumption tag [Fox, Quantum Optics (2006)]. The next section moves into electrical injection and edge-emitting device physics, where the pump itself becomes a quantum-statistical input rather than a rate constant.
